title: Friends above all
hook: Epicurus: of all wisdom provides for a happy life, the greatest is friendship (Principal Doctrines 27)

segments.voice: Yesterday: Lucretius, who pictured the time after death as a mirror of before birth. Your line was where death is, I'm not. What did you finish from the unfinished list? Day six hundred fifty-three.

Before you choose a restaurant, do you think about the food, or about who's coming? Epicurus had a firm answer. Seneca, the Stoic, passes it on in one of his letters: look first for whom you'll eat and drink with, before you look at what you'll eat and drink. Eating alone, without a friend, he says, is the life of a lion or a wolf. Strong words from a man known for simple food. Today, the Garden's center. Principal Doctrines.
screen: `THE FOOD, OR WHO'S COMING?` → `FIRST: WHOM YOU'LL EAT WITH.` → `FRIENDS ABOVE ALL.`

segments.voice: First, the doctrine. Epicurus left a set of short sayings, the Principal Doctrines. Number twenty-seven says, in plain words: of all the things wisdom provides for a happy life, by far the greatest is friendship. Out of everything wisdom provides, friends come first. Second, why a philosopher of pleasure ranks it first. Epicurus said a friendship may begin from need: someone helps you, you help them. But it becomes worth having for its own sake. And it carries something else: confidence. Another saying of his puts it this way: it isn't so much our friends' help that helps us, as our trust that they'd help if we needed it. That trust takes a great deal of fear out of life. Third, how the Garden lived it. Diogenes Laërtius says Epicurus had so many friends that whole cities couldn't count them. In his will, which Diogenes Laërtius preserves, Epicurus provided for his birthday to be kept every year, for his students to meet together every month, and for the children of his friend Metrodorus, who had died. Fourth, the neighbor's answer. The Stoics also prized friendship, but they called it a good only between people of virtue, and wanted the wise person to be able to stand alone if friends were lost. Epicurus wanted friendship close to the center of the good life. Two schools, both serious about friends, weighting them differently. And either way, a good meal with no one across the table was, to Epicurus, hardly a meal at all.
screen: `PRINCIPAL DOCTRINE 27.` · `TRUST THAT THEY'D HELP.` · `TOO MANY FRIENDS TO COUNT.` · `THE STOICS WEIGHED IT DIFFERENTLY.` · then, large: `FRIENDSHIP FIRST.`

segments.voice: Settle, and breathe. Let a few friends come to mind, one at a time, no ranking. Now settle on one you trust, someone who would help if you needed it. Epicurus said that trust does more for us than the help itself. Stay with that person's face for a moment. Then ask: when did I last make time for them? Not a quick message. Time. Let a day and a place come to mind. The bell holds the time.
Principal Doctrines. Epicurus's short sayings, number twenty-seven of which calls friendship the greatest gift wisdom provides for a happy life. Today's word.
Your line: friendship first. Make time for one friend today, even ten minutes on the phone, with nothing else going on. Day six hundred fifty-three.

howItsDone: Epicureans, ancient and modern, place friendship at the center of a good life, sharing meals, keeping in touch and caring for one another's families.

notes: Editor review 2026-10-01: cut the count 'forty' and 'meant to be memorized'; replaced the vague 'ate together, kept birthdays' with what the will in DL 10.18 actually provides (birthday kept yearly, monthly meeting, Metrodorus's children); dropped 'who loved to quote him' so tomorrow's Seneca angle isn't taken; practice no longer tells the listener what they feel and now works VS 34 (trust) instead of repeating day 650's message-a-friend carry.
Forty Principal Doctrines (Kyriai Doxai) preserved in DL 10.139–154. Confirm count.
Seneca, Letter 19.10: look for whom to eat with before what to eat; dining without a friend is the life of a lion or wolf. Paraphrased; confirm.
VS 34: not so much our friends' help as confidence in their help. VS 23: friendship begins from benefit, desirable for itself. Confirm numbering.
DL 10.9: friends so many they couldn't be counted by whole cities. Will: yearly gatherings and provision for Metrodorus's children (DL 10.16–21). Confirm.
Stoic view of friendship (only among the virtuous; the sage self-sufficient) simplified; confirm fair.
